title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling Playbook, Benchmarks, Runbooks and Known Issues
author: Avery Patel
content:
Summary:

This consolidated reference documents Redwood Inference's serving runtime: architecture overview, kernel scheduling design, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, release notes highlights, known issues with mitigations, operational runbooks (on-call and triage), and the runtime team wiki pointers. The goal is a single authoritative page for engineers and SREs to onboard, diagnose, and evolve the serving runtime.

Scope:
- Production inference runtime (hosted, Dedicated, Private)
- Components: dispatcher, scheduler, kernel executor, KV-cache, batching manager, telemetry/metrics, and rollout/fallback logic
- Excludes: client SDKs, API surface, and Dedicated hardware procurement details (see related pages)

Owner and contacts:
- Primary owner: runtime-team@redwood.example.com (runtime-service)
- On-call rotation: eng-sre (tier-0), runtime on-call (tier-1)
- Primary maintainers: Avery Patel (author), Jordan Kim (profiling/benchmarks), María Gómez (kernel scheduling)

Architecture overview:
1) High-level components:
   - Dispatcher: receives API requests, performs input validation, routing decisions (region, cost tier, fallback model)
   - Per-model Scheduler: maintains request queues, implements latency-aware batching policies and cache affinity
   - Kernel Executor: GPU/CPU execution layer; selects compiled kernels and quantization execution path per layer
   - KV Cache Manager: prefix/KV cache for repeated context reuse with LRU eviction and per-tenant TTLs
   - Batching Service: continuous batching loop with dynamic batching windows driven by SLOs and request characteristics
   - Observability: metrics, tracing, p95/p99 latency histograms, token-level cost reporting, and per-route error counters

2) Key design principles:
   - Latency-first SLOs: tail latency (p99) is primary; batching and cache are tuned to minimize p99 impact while reducing cost
   - Model-variant fallbacks: automatic routing to significantly cheaper/quantized variants when capacity constrained
   - Deterministic scheduling: prefer deterministic heuristics for fairness and reproducibility across runs

Kernel scheduling and selection:
- Goals: maximize GPU utilization, minimize kernel launch overhead, and keep KV cache locality intact.
- Execution modes:
  1. Low-latency mode: aggressive single-request priority, small batch sizes (batch_size <= 8), kernel path optimized for minimal startup overhead
  2. Throughput mode: larger batching (batch_size up to 256 depending on sequence length and memory), grouped kernel launches, fused attention kernels where available
  3. Hybrid mode: per-route SLO-based adaptive switching (runtime monitors latency and switches mode per-model or per-tenant)

Scheduling heuristics (per-model scheduler):
- Priority lanes: realtime, interactive, background (training-like), and prefetch. Each lane maps to target p50/p95 SLOs.
- Affinity-based placement: requests with common KV prefixes are co-scheduled to increase cache hit rates.
- Cost-aware packing: schedule requests by token-length histogram to reduce padding and maximize packed batch utilization.
- Preemption policy: realtime lane preempts background lane when p95 latency exceeds threshold for two consecutive windows (window=1s).

Profiling playbook (how to profile a performance regression):
Purpose: reproducibly measure and triage runtime performance regressions and changes in token/latency/cost characteristics.

1) Preparation:
   - Identify the regression signal(s): increased p50/p95, higher GPU utilization with worse latency, or higher per-token cost
   - Collect context: deployment id, model/version, config (batching, quantization profile), region, recent deploys, and request traces for the timeframe

2) Data collection (commands and targets):
   - Metrics: query Prometheus for 1h and 24h windows for metrics: runtime_p50, runtime_p95, runtime_p99, kernel_launch_latency_ms, batch_size_distribution, kv_cache_hit_rate, gpu_utilization_per_card.
     Example: curl -s "https://prometheus/api/v1/query_range?query=runtime_p95&start=..."
   - Traces: use distributed tracing UI and export full traces for 10-50 representative requests.
   - Perf traces: capture nvprof/ Nsight or ROCm SMI sample for 60s on impacted nodes (coordinate with infra to run in isolated window).
   - Core dumps: if OOM or segfaults occurred, collect dmesg and /var/crash artifacts.

3) Reproduce locally/in-staging:
   - Use the benchmark harness (see Benchmarking suite below) with recorded trace files to replay realistic arrival patterns and input-length distributions.
   - Disable autoscaling and run with identical capacity to affected prod region when possible.

4) Narrow root cause:
   - Compare kernel selection distributions (which kernels used per layer) between baseline and regressed run. Differences often point to compiler/quantization changes or kernel library regressions.
   - Examine batching windows and late arrivals; high variance in arrival times can cause smaller effective batches and higher per-token latency.
   - Inspect KV cache hit/miss ratios — a drop in hit rate can spike runtime due to more KV recomputation.

5) Mitigation steps (temporary):
   - Rollback the suspect release or pin model to earlier variant
   - Force scheduler into low-latency mode for realtime lanes to protect tail latency
   - Increase dedicated capacity or adjust autoscaler policies to smooth out backpressure

6) Long-term fixes:
   - Kernel recompile with improved heuristics or fallbacks; file ticket with kernel-engineering and include perf artifacts
   - Improve request routing to preserve cache affinity and reduce inter-node KV misses
   - Add more deterministic batching tests to CI harnessing the benchmark suite

Benchmarking suite (what we run and how):
- Purpose: automated regression detection and capacity planning. Benchmarks run in CI and nightly/weekly scheduled suites.
- Components:
  1. Microbenchmarks: per-kernel latency and memory footprint (single-threaded and multi-stream)
  2. Model-level perf: per-model end-to-end token throughput for common open models (e.g., RedLM-3B, RedLM-13B, RedLM-70B) across sequence lengths [128, 512, 2048]
  3. Arrival-pattern tests: Poisson, burst, and steady-state to measure batching window behavior and tail latency
  4. KV-cache stress tests: synthetic workloads with repeated prefixes to validate cache hit improvements and eviction behavior
  5. Quantization profile matrix: run models across INT8/FP16/FP32 variants and record quality/cost tradeoffs

- Example benchmark matrix (table):

  Benchmark, Target HW, Sequence lengths, Mode, Primary metrics
  "microkernel-latency", "A100-80GB", "n/a", "single-request", "latency_ms, p99_ms, memory_mb"
  "redlm-13b-throughput", "A100-80GB", "128/512/2048", "throughput", "tokens/s, cost_per_token_usd, p99_latency_ms"
  "arrival-burst-test", "T4-16GB", "512", "burst", "p50/p95/p99 latency, batch_size_dist"

- Running benchmarks:
  - CI: quick microbenchmarks (fast) as pre-merge checks for kernel/compiler changes
  - Nightly: full model matrix with 95% fidelity configs and auto-generated reports uploaded to perf dashboard
  - Capacity run: weekly large-scale runs to model cost curves and capacity planning (run by eng-infra)

- Reporting:
  - Perf dashboard stores historical trends and alerts on >10% regression in tokens/s or >15% regression in p99 latency for any model/sequence combination

Release notes (recent highlights):
- 2027-11-01 (v2.9.0): Introduced hybrid scheduling mode and affinity-aware placement. Improved batch packing heuristic to reduce wasted tokens by ~12% in our internal e-commerce workload.
- 2027-12-08 (v2.9.3): Backported kernel fallback to avoid a rare fused attention regression on ROCm stacks; fixed crash in KV-eviction path under high-churn tenants.
- 2028-01-05 (v3.0.0-alpha): Experimental INT8 quant path for RedLM-13B with accuracy guardrails; performance improvements of 2.2x tokens/s in throughput mode on A100.

Known issues and mitigations (operational):
1) Intermittent p99 spikes when mixed large and small sequence-length traffic coexists
   - Symptom: p99 latency increases by 2-4x for 1-3 minute windows, correlated with a drop in batch_size mean
   - Root cause: scheduler packs by arrival time and sometimes fails to pack similar-length requests together under bursty patterns
   - Mitigation: enable length-based bucketing for affected routes and pin to hybrid mode during business hours
   - Long-term: integrate sequence-length-aware admission control into scheduler

2) ROCm fused-kernel occasional miscompile on kernel library v1.14.2
   - Symptom: rare kernel errors and fallback to slower generic kernels (higher latency)
   - Workaround: force fallback to legacy kernel path via runtime flag until vendor patch is available (flag: KERNEL_LEGACY_FALLBACK=true)

3) KV-cache hot-tenant eviction storms
   - Symptom: short-lived increase in RPCs to backend and higher end-to-end latency for eviction-affected tenants
   - Mitigation: tune tenant TTLs and increase cache capacity for read-heavy tenants; near-term: apply tenant-specific cache reservation

Runtime runbooks (triage and mitigation):
- On-call quick checklist:
  1. Confirm alert: examine perf dashboard and match to runbook conditions (p99>target for 5m)
  2. Identify scope: single node, single AZ, model-wide, or customer-specific
  3. Check autoscaler events and recent deploys (git sha pinned in deployment metadata)
  4. Toggle safeguards: switch to low-latency scheduler for affected routes; escalate to infra to add capacity if autoscaler is saturated
  5. If crash/OOM: collect core, increase coredump retention, and open sev ticket linking to crash artifacts

- Detailed investigation steps (for SRE/runtime engineer):
  - Collect 30-minute windows of detailed metrics and traces.
  - Run reproduce script in staging using the benchmark harness: tools/bench/replay_trace.py --trace <trace.json> --concurrency <n>
  - If kernel-level issue suspected, coordinate with kernel-eng: attach nvprof/Nsight logs, kernel names, and environment (CUDA/ROCm versions)

Team wiki and knowledge base pointers:
- Primary runtime wiki index: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/serving-runtime-team-wiki-playbook-2027-11-20
- Benchmarks and CI jobs: gitlab.com/redwood-inference/runtime/perf-ci (internal)
- Kernel-engineering contact: #kernel-eng on Slack; cirrus ticket template: /templates/kernel-perf-issue.md
- Observability dashboards: grafana.redwood/runtime-perf, traces.redwood/jaeger-runtime

Configuration examples and snippets:
- Example per-model scheduler config (YAML):
  model: redlm-13b
  lanes:
    - name: realtime
      target_p95_ms: "120"
      max_batch_size: "8"
    - name: throughput
      target_tokens_s: "20000"
      max_batch_size: "256"
  affinity: true
  kv_cache_ttl_s: "3600"

- Example CLI to run the arrival-pattern benchmark:
  tools/bench/run_benchmark.sh --model redlm-13b --pattern burst --duration 300 --hw a100-80gb

Quality and testing guidance:
- Add microkernel unit tests for any kernel changes; include deterministic inputs and golden latency expectations
- For scheduler changes, add simulation tests in the scheduler-sim harness to ensure fairness and cache-affinity are preserved across synthetic workloads
- Bench PR gating: any change modifying kernel selection, quantization, or scheduler packing must include CI microbenchmarks and a request to run the nightly full benchmark matrix before merge for high-risk repos

Appendix A: Useful queries and commands:
- Prometheus p95 query: runtime_p95{model="redlm-13b"}[5m]
- List running kernels on node: nvidia-smi -q -d PIDS,UTILIZATION
- Capture Nsight (example): nsight-sys -o /tmp/profile.qdrep --capture-range=process:start,end --target-pid <pid>

Appendix B: Change log (high level):
- 2027-11-01: v2.9.0 hybrid scheduling enabled
- 2027-12-08: v2.9.3 ROCm fallback patch and KV-eviction fixes
- 2028-01-05: v3.0.0-alpha INT8 experimental path

Appendix C: Ownership & escalation matrix:
- Pager: eng-sre (primary), runtime@redwood.example.com (secondary)
- Level 1: on-call runtime engineer (10-30 min response SLA)
- Level 2: runtime lead and kernel-eng (30-60 min)
- Level 3: CTO/infra exec escalation (>60 min)

If you are updating this document:
1) Add a short summary of the change with date and author at the bottom of the page.
2) Add reviewers if changes touch kernel selection or scheduler defaults.
3) For breaking changes, include a migration plan and a rollback playbook.

Related pages and further reading are listed in the metadata above. For questions, contact the runtime owners or open an issue in the internal tracking board (runtime-team backlog).
